<reason>Side A systematically dismantled every pillar of Side B's case. First, Side A exposed a fatal contradiction in Side B's opening: because decriminalizing possession leaves supply illegal, it neither purifies contaminated drugs nor lowers black-market prices driving theft—forcing Side B to walk back those claims in Rebuttal 2. Second, Side A neutralized Side B's remaining advantages (fear of calling 911 and criminal records blocking employment) by pointing to Good Samaritan laws and drug courts that expunge records upon treatment completion, points Side B neglected until its final speech. Finally, Side A won the micro-clashes on fentanyl's destruction of rational agency, selection bias in voluntary rehab statistics, and how legalizing street-level possession strips police of the probable cause needed to search dealers.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>In [A4.3]-[A4.5], Side A locked in Side B's concession that decriminalization leaves street drugs toxic and expensive, showed that Good Samaritan laws and drug-court expungements already solve Side B's remaining harms, and refuted Side B's claim that police can still prosecute dealers using "scales, cash, communications" [B4.2] by explaining that legalizing open possession removes the probable cause required to stop and search suspects for those items in the first place.</best_rebuttal>
